message.content:
Two related features for Nxeon's custom VPS/game-server builder ("Build a custom server" in the deploy wizard, `lib/custom-plan.ts` + `lib/custom-plan-pricing.ts` + `components/nx/CustomServer.tsx`/`DeployView.tsx`). Work in a fresh isolated git worktree off current `main` in `/opt/nxeon` (e.g. `git worktree add /root/nxeon-worktrees/custom-plan-intro-sales -b feature/custom-plan-intro-and-sales-fallback main`) — never work directly in `/opt/nxeon`, never run `npm run build` there (explicit house rule, already violated once today with real prod consequences).

## Context you need first

Today custom builds (both VPS `createCustomPlan` and per-game `createCustomGamePlan` in `lib/custom-plan.ts`) got a real per-resource pricing overhaul — every family now has an honest, data-derived rate. That work is already merged into `main`. Read `lib/custom-plan.ts` and `lib/custom-plan-pricing.ts` in full before touching anything — you need to understand `createCustomPlan`, `createCustomGamePlan`, `customPlanQuote`, `customGamePlanQuote`, `customPlanCapacityCheck`, and the `CreatedCustomPlan`/`CreatedCustomGamePlan` return shapes.

## Feature 1: 30% intro price on custom builds, matching the existing catalog convention exactly

**Confirmed with the owner**: every currently active `Plan` and `GamePlan` in the real catalog (checked live: VPS Starter/Standard/Pro/Max, and ARK/Minecraft/Rust/Squad tiers) has `introPriceCents` set to almost exactly 69.5% of `priceCents` (≈30% off) with `introTermMonths: null` (the discount covers the WHOLE first term, any length, not just month one — see `Plan.introPriceCents`'s schema doc comment and `GamePlan.introPriceCents`'s, which mirrors it). This is a real, consistent, deliberate site-wide policy — not something you're inventing.

Custom builds currently get NONE of this: `createCustomPlan`/`createCustomGamePlan`'s `db.plan.create`/`db.gamePlan.create` calls never set `introPriceCents`/`introTermMonths`, so a custom order's first charge and its renewal charge (frozen via `Server.grandfatheredRenewalCents`, which already works correctly for custom orders — don't touch that mechanism) are identical, with no discount.

**What to build**: when creating a custom `Plan`/`GamePlan` row, also compute and set `introPriceCents = round(priceCents × 0.70)` (30% off — make the exact percentage an admin-tunable setting, e.g. `custom_plan_intro_percent` in `lib/settings.ts`, default 30, read the same way `lib/settings.ts`'s other `getSettingInt` calls work in this file already) and `introTermMonths: null`.

**Critical — this must reach the wizard's own live preview, not just the final charge.** Read `lib/order.ts`'s `orderQuote` (around line 390-435) and `lib/game-order.ts`'s equivalent (around line 400-410) to see EXACTLY how intro pricing is computed and surfaced today for premade plans (`introFirstTermDiscountCents`, `introSoldPercent`, the `promo` object with `"Intro price — renews at $X/mo"` copy, `Server.termPromoPercent`). This exact machinery is generic — it already works for ANY `Plan`/`GamePlan` row with `introPriceCents` set, premade or custom, with ZERO changes needed to `orderQuote`/`placeOrder`/`gameOrderQuote`/`placeGameOrder` themselves, SINCE those functions read the resolved `Plan`/`GamePlan` row from the DB — once your custom row has real `introPriceCents`, checkout naturally shows and charges the discounted first term and freezes the regular price as the renewal rate. Verify this claim yourself by reading the code, don't assume it — if something about capacity checks, coupon stacking, or annual-discount interaction near that code path treats a `sortOrder: 999` custom row differently, find it and handle it.

The part that needs REAL new work: `components/nx/CustomServer.tsx`'s live slider preview and its "authoritative" debounced quote check (`quoteCustomPlanAction`/`quoteCustomGamePlanAction`/`customPlanQuote`/`customGamePlanQuote` — the PREVIEW path, separate from the checkout path) currently only computes and shows the flat regular price. This is the EXACT bug class found and fixed earlier today in this same feature (a customer watching a wrong price the whole time they move the sliders, then a different number at checkout) — do not reintroduce it. The preview must show the SAME intro price / "renews at $X" split the real checkout will charge, computed the identical way. Trace how a PREMADE tier's card currently shows its own intro price in the wizard (there's existing UI for this somewhere in `components/nx/DeployView.tsx` or `CustomServer.tsx` — a tier card showing "$X first term, renews at $Y/mo" or similar) and reuse that same display pattern for the custom builder's live preview, not a new one.

## Feature 2: when a custom spec exceeds real node capacity, offer a sales-lead path instead of a dead end

**The problem, in the owner's words**: "the custom servers says the host doesnt have enough resources which makes us look smaller. so instead if someone is customizing a massive server that we cant support an auto deploy on, so they have an option to contact sales / support ticket that carries that specs they want."

The exact failure point today: `lib/custom-plan.ts`'s `customPlanCapacityCheck` returns `{ ok: false, reason: "No node currently has room for a server this size. Please contact support." }` (line ~282) when no node has room — this is a real, correct guard (never let a customer buy something that can't actually be provisioned), but today it's a dead-end error with no actual path forward.

**What to build**: when the deploy wizard's custom-builder hits this specific capacity-exceeded case (both VPS and game — check where this surfaces in `app/dashboard/deploy/page.tsx`/`lib/actions-custom-plan.ts`'s server actions and the UI in `components/nx/CustomServer.tsx`), instead of (or alongside) the bare error, offer a real "Contact sales" action that creates a real support ticket via `lib/actions-support.ts`'s `createTicket`, prefilled with:
- The exact spec the customer configured (vCPU, RAM, disk, game family if applicable, any other relevant CustomServer builder state)
- Framed as a real sales inquiry (e.g. subject like "Custom server request — needs review" or similar honest framing, not implying it's already been provisioned)

Read `lib/actions-support.ts`'s `createTicket` signature and the `Ticket` model in `prisma/schema.prisma` to build this correctly — it's a normal `"use server"` action taking `FormData`, so you'll need a real form/button in the wizard UI wired to it, not just a backend function. Match this codebase's existing UI conventions for this kind of contextual CTA (look at how `CustomServer.tsx` already handles its "Talk to sales" escalation past the self-serve ceiling, mentioned in today's earlier changelog entry — there may already be a similar pattern to extend rather than invent from scratch).

## Process (same as everything else that shipped today)

1. Read before writing. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean in your isolated worktree before considering anything done.
2. Verify against real data: this is a real money-path change (intro pricing affects what customers are charged). Query real prod data (read-only) to confirm your 30%-off computation matches the existing catalog's actual ratio precisely for a few real plans, and run a real Stripe test-mode checkout (staging, `sk_test_...`) proving quoted === created === charged for at least one VPS custom case and one game custom case, both showing the discounted first-term price and the correct frozen renewal rate — matching the verification rigor the per-family pricing branch used earlier today (real Stripe PaymentIntents, not a hand-calculation).
3. For feature 2, verify the actual ticket gets created with the right prefilled spec — a real ticket row in the DB, not just no errors.
4. Deploy to staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh <branch>`) and actually look at both changes — screenshot or describe what you verified. This codebase's own CLAUDE.md is explicit that a change which typechecks can still be visibly broken.
5. Update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` (dated changelog entry, required house rule) and `ROADMAP.md`.
6. Push your branch. Do NOT merge into main or promote to production — this is a real pricing change, the owner should see the diff first. Say so clearly in your report along with the branch name.

Report back with: confirmation the 30% intro price is now correctly shown in both the wizard preview AND the final charge (with real Stripe verification numbers), confirmation the capacity-exceeded sales-lead flow creates a real ticket with the right spec, and the branch name.

---
name: nxeon-build-isolation
description: "NEVER run npm run build (or agent builds) in the live prod tree /opt/nxeon — it clobbers prod's .next and breaks the site"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc
  modified: 2026-08-11T05:24:18.217Z
---

**NEVER run `npm run build` in the live prod working tree `/opt/nxeon`.** nxeon-web serves `/opt/nxeon/.next` and nxeon-worker runs `tsx worker/index.ts` off the same tree. A build there overwrites `.next` (new chunk hashes) while the OLD server process keeps running → browser requests chunks by hashes that no longer exist → `ChunkLoadError` / "Something went wrong" on every page (esp. /admin). Also `git checkout <branch>` in the prod tree switches the worker's live code.

**Why:** 2026-08-10 overnight run — I spawned build agents as normal general-purpose agents that `git checkout -b` + `npm run build` INSIDE /opt/nxeon. Each build clobbered prod's compiled assets; prod admin threw ChunkLoadError for hours. Fix was: stop the agent, `git checkout <last-promoted-commit>`, `npm run build`, `chown -R nxeon:nxeon .next`, `systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker`, then hard-refresh the browser.

**How to apply:** build/verify agents MUST work in an ISOLATED git worktree (Agent `isolation: "worktree"`, or manual `git worktree add`) or in `/opt/nxeon-staging` — NEVER the prod tree. The prod tree `/opt/nxeon` should stay parked at the currently-deployed commit; only `scripts/promote-production.sh` (build+restart) moves prod, and only on explicit user authorization. Staging builds go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` which operates on `/opt/nxeon-staging`. See [[nxeon-ventures-hub]], [[nxeon-platform]].
---
name: nxeon-worktree-nodemodules-hazard
description: "NEVER git add -A in a worktree that has a node_modules symlink — it can destroy prod's real node_modules"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc
  modified: 2026-08-21T17:19:08.560Z
---

On 2026-08-21 I nearly took prod down. In a worktree I created `node_modules` as a symlink to `/opt/nxeon/node_modules` (the standard setup), then ran `git add -A` which COMMITTED the symlink (`.gitignore` has `node_modules/` with a trailing slash, which does NOT match a symlink named `node_modules`). Fast-forwarding that commit into the prod tree `/opt/nxeon` replaced its **real** `node_modules` directory with a **self-referential symlink** (`/opt/nxeon/node_modules -> /opt/nxeon/node_modules`), deleting 1.1G of packages. `next` and the Prisma client became unresolvable; only the in-memory running services survived.

**Why:** never stage the whole tree in a symlinked worktree.
**How to apply:**
- In worktrees, `git add` ONLY the specific files you changed — never `git add -A` / `git add .`.
- Recovery if it happens: `git rm --cached node_modules && rm -f node_modules` in the prod tree, then `npm ci` (lockfile present) + `npx prisma generate`, then commit the untracking. Do this BEFORE any restart/promote — running services hold modules in memory but a build/restart will fail hard.
- Consider hardening `.gitignore` with a bare `node_modules` line (no slash) so the symlink is ignored too.

Relates to [[nxeon-build-isolation]] and the deploy flow in [[nxeon-resume-point]].

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. The one exception is a workshop document from the `workshop` skill, which carries its own design: there Claude skips `artifact-design` and loads `artifact-diagramming` for a template page's diagrams. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com or cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/ (the skill has the full list) and stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- If the file is outside the working directory, you must Read it in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.

---
name: nxeon-disk-full-outage-2026-09-27
description: Primary node root disk hit 100% from build caches, Postgres crashed, prod 500 for ~10 min; what to clear and what never to touch
metadata:
  type: project
---

**2026-09-27, 08:21–08:31 UTC:** the primary node's root filesystem filled up and production went down.
- **Symptom:** `/dev/md3` (49G, `/`) reached 100%. `postgresql@17-main`, which holds prod `nxeon` plus the staging DBs, crashed with "No space left on device", and prod on :3000 returned 500.
- **Cause:** cumulative regenerable caches, not the databases (all DBs together are about 500 MB).
  - staging `.next/cache` (2.1G)
  - `~/.npm/_cacache` (1.7G), `~/.cache/go-build` (1.3G)
  - worktree `.next` build outputs (2.2G in `ssh-management-key`)
  - The trigger was the /nxm `next dev` cache growing during multi-agent work.
- **Fix:** delete those caches, then `systemctl start postgresql@17-main` (it crash-recovers cleanly). That took free space from 134M to 8.5G.

**How to apply:**
- Before long builds or multi-agent `next dev` sessions on this box, check `df -h /`.
- Safe to clear: `~/.npm/_cacache`, `~/.cache/go-build`, `<tree>/.next/cache`, and `.next` of merged worktrees that no process uses (check with `lsof +D`).
- Never touch: `/var/lib/vz`, `/tank`, DB files, `/opt/nxeon/.next`, or the standalone output in `/opt/nxeon-staging/.next`.
- A follow-up task was offered to add disk alerting.

Related: [[nxeon-build-isolation]], [[nxeon-node1-cpu-and-devapp-relocation]].

#!/bin/bash
# Deploy a ref (default: main from /opt/nxeon) to the staging environment.
# Usage: ./scripts/deploy-staging.sh [git-ref]
set -euo pipefail
REF="${1:-main}"
cd /opt/nxeon-staging

echo "==> Syncing staging to $REF"
git fetch origin
git reset --hard "origin/$REF"

echo "==> Installing dependencies"
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -1

echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss 2>&1 | tail -2
npm run db:seed 2>&1 | tail -2 || true

echo "==> Building"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4

# next.config sets output:"standalone" but the systemd unit runs the standalone
# server.js directly (not `next start`, which Next.js explicitly does not
# support alongside output:"standalone" — it prints a warning and silently
# fails to resolve some routes, confirmed live 2026-09-10: a brand-new API
# route 404'd under `next start` on this exact build and returned 200 under
# `node .next/standalone/server.js`). The standalone output does NOT include
# public/ or .next/static/ (Next's own documented behavior) — copy them in
# fresh every build, or every static asset/route added after the last copy
# is missing until the next deploy happens to also touch this step.
echo "==> Copying static assets into the standalone server output"
rm -rf .next/standalone/public .next/standalone/.next/static
cp -r public .next/standalone/public
cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/static
# geoip-lite is in next.config.ts's serverExternalPackages (kept OUT of the JS
# bundle on purpose, since it reads .dat files off its own package path at
# runtime) — but the standalone output tracer only copies files it can trace
# as JS-imported, so an externalized package's own non-JS data files are
# silently left behind. Found live 2026-09-10: this crashed EVERY request
# with an uncaught ENOENT the moment the systemd unit ran the standalone
# server.js instead of `next start` — geo-ip.ts's own try/catch around
# geoip.lookup() does NOT help, because the failure isn't confined to that
# call. Copy the package's real data/ directory in every build, same
# reasoning as public/.next/static above.
if [ -d node_modules/geoip-lite/data ]; then
  mkdir -p .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data
  cp -r node_modules/geoip-lite/data/. .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data/
fi

# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. Only .next needs to be writable by
# it (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable, and systemd
# injects .env as root. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon-staging/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon-staging/.env 2>/dev/null || true

echo "==> Restarting staging services"
systemctl restart nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
echo "==> Staging responds: HTTP $CODE (http://$(grep ^PUBLIC_IP .env | cut -d= -f2):8080)"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "STAGING UNHEALTHY"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Staging deploy complete"

1	# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform
2	
3	Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).
4	
5	## Architecture
6	
7	- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
8	- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
9	- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
10	- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
11	- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
12	- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).
13	
14	## Portals & design system
15	
16	**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.
17	
18	- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
19	  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
20	  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
21	  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).
22	
23	- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
24	  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
25	  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
26	  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).
27	
28	- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
29	  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
30	  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
31	  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
32	  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
33	  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
34	  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
35	  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.
36	
37	- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
38	- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
39	- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).
40	
41	## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session
42	
43	`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.
44	
45	1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
46	2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
47	3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
48	4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
49	5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.
50	
51	If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).
52	
53	## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)
54	
55	- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). Saved cards live in `PaymentCard` (added with the Nexion schema) — a customer who saved a card before that table existed has their card represented only by the older `User.stripeCustomerId`/`stripePaymentMethodId` columns; `hasChargeableCard`/renewals read those directly and are unaffected, but the Billing page's card list reads `PaymentCard`, so a pre-existing card needs the one-off backfill (`scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts`) to show up there. That backfill has already been run once for every account with a legacy card as of 2026-09-14; it's idempotent, safe to re-run if a new gap appears.
56	- **Namecheap** (`lib/namecheap.ts`): `NAMECHEAP_API_USER/KEY/USERNAME/CLIENT_IP` (+`NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX=1` for testing) → domain search/register/renew/DNS management. TLD retail prices in `TLD_PRICES`.
57	- **GitHub**: remote `origin` = `git@github.com:santino1233/nxeon.git` via deploy key `/root/.ssh/nxeon_deploy`. Every commit auto-pushes via `.git/hooks/post-commit`. `.env`/credentials are gitignored — never commit secrets.
58	
59	## Conventions
60	
61	- All state changes to VMs go through `Job` rows — the web app never calls Proxmox mutation endpoints directly (read-only status calls are OK).
62	- One in-flight job per server (enforced in `serverAction`).
63	- Admin-only actions live in [lib/actions.ts](lib/actions.ts) and must call `requireAdmin()`.
64	- Free VPSes: `Server.isFree = true`, no billing, `expiresAt = null`.
65	- Wallet amounts are integer cents.
66	- Never fabricate: no invented stats, ratings, reviews, player counts, or ETAs. If a number can't be read from the database or a real upstream, the field stays empty and the UI says why — this tree has had hash-derived star ratings and fake reviews removed once already.
67	- Minecraft subdomains (`*.play.nxeon.cloud`) are shared across two tables — `FreeMinecraftServer.subdomain` and `Server.subdomain` — because both products resolve under the same DNS zone. Always check availability through `lib/game-subdomain.ts`'s `isSubdomainAvailable()` (queries both) rather than checking either table alone, or a free and a paid server can claim the same name.
68	
69	## Documentation — keep it current (required)
70	
71	- **Every change, fix, or addition MUST update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` in the same commit.** Add a dated bullet to §15 (Change history) and edit any section the change affects (data model, subsystems, feature catalog, integrations, roadmap, etc.). A commit that changes behaviour without touching the docs is incomplete.
72	- Keep `ROADMAP.md` in sync too: check off / move the item you completed.
73	- `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` is the single source of truth. The public mirror at `https://revsports.ca/docs` is regenerated from it with `node scripts/publish-docs.mjs` (zero-dep markdown→styled-HTML renderer → `/var/www/nxeon-docs/index.html`) — run that after editing the doc so the hosted page matches. The `/docs` nginx location lives in `scripts/configure-domains.sh` so it survives vhost regeneration.
74	- The claude.ai artifact webpage (`https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9b0c97f5-4c34-4f89-bee9-b5a80eb23892`) can only be updated from an interactive Claude Code session (headless/cron runs can't reach it) — that refresh is best-effort, the repo doc + `/docs` page are authoritative.
75	
76	## Commands
77	
78	- Typecheck: `npx tsc --noEmit` (always, before a build)
79	- Build: `npm run build` (must pass before restarting services)
80	- Deploy after changes: `npm run build && systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker` — or, preferably, go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `scripts/promote-production.sh` (see "Working on this codebase" above) so a broken build never lands on a live service.
81	- Worker logs: `journalctl -u nxeon-worker -f`
82	- E2E test: `npx tsx scripts/e2e-test.ts` (orders a real VM; delete it afterwards via a DELETE job)
83	- Admin credentials: `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt`
84	
85	## Domains & TLS
86	
87	- **Single source of truth**: `/etc/nxeon/domains.env` (BASE_DOMAIN, ADMIN_HOST, STAGING_HOST, CERTBOT_EMAIL). The domain is a placeholder (`revsports.ca`) until the real one is bought. **Never hardcode the domain anywhere in app code** — the app uses `APP_URL` / `NXEON_ADMIN_HOST` from `.env`, and nginx vhosts are generated.
88	- **To migrate to a new domain**: edit `/etc/nxeon/domains.env`, point DNS (A records for apex, www, admin host, staging host) at the server, then run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It regenerates nginx vhosts, obtains Let's Encrypt certs, updates APP_URL in both `.env`s, and restarts web. That's the whole migration.
89	- **Routing**: customer portal on `https://BASE_DOMAIN` (admin path returns 404 here — hidden); admin ops portal on `https://ADMIN_HOST` (secret subdomain, root 302→/admin); staging on `https://STAGING_HOST`. HTTP→HTTPS 301. Real LE cert (auto-renews via certbot timer); self-signed fallback for bare-IP. A raw `http://51.79.162.96:8080` fallback listener also exists for staging (no TLS, no forwarded headers) — it's a debug path only, not how a real customer or any Server Action's origin check expects to be reached; testing against it directly produces false failures (CSP/origin-check errors) that don't reproduce on the real `STAGING_HOST`.
90	- Secure cookies are on (`COOKIE_SECURE=1`) now that real HTTPS exists. Stripe webhook is live at `https://BASE_DOMAIN/api/stripe/webhook`.
91	
92	## Environments
93	
94	- **Production**: `/opt/nxeon`, DB `nxeon`, services `nxeon-web` (port 3000) + `nxeon-worker`, nginx port 80, VPS pools IP 10.20.0.100–250 / SSH ports 20000–29999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD`. Public: http://51.79.162.96
95	- **Staging**: `/opt/nxeon-staging`, DB `nxeon_staging`, services `nxeon-staging-web` (port 3001) + `nxeon-staging-worker`, nginx port 8080, ISOLATED VPS pools IP 10.20.0.50–99 / SSH ports 30000–30999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD_STG`, VM tag `nxeon-staging`. Public: http://51.79.162.96:8080 (see the TLS note above — prefer `STAGING_HOST` over the bare port for anything that exercises real form submissions). Admin creds: `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt`.
96	- **node-2 sandbox** (optional, not required): `nxeon-fsn1` (178.63.94.114), tree at `/opt/nxeon-v2`, its own DB (`nxeon_v2`), `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` (stubs Proxmox provisioning + Stripe charges only — everything else is real code against a real, separate DB). Useful for large or highly experimental work in isolation; not part of the normal edit→stage→promote path above. Root SSH from node-2 to this box exists (`scripts/node1.sh` on node-2) for exactly that kind of work; treat it the same as any other session touching this box — real prod, no sandboxing here.
97	- Instance differences are driven entirely by `.env` (NXEON_ENV, NXEON_COOKIE_NAME, NXEON_NAT_CHAIN, NXEON_TAG, NXEON_IP_START/END, NXEON_SSH_PORT_START/END, NXEON_CRED_FILE, PORT, APP_URL) — the code is identical.
98	- **Deploy flow**: push to GitHub → `scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]` builds+migrates+restarts staging → verify at `STAGING_HOST` (or `:8080`, with the TLS caveat above) → `scripts/promote-production.sh` rebuilds+restarts production. Test changes on staging before promoting — always.
99	
100	## Safety rules
101	
102	- NEVER touch VMIDs 9000–9999 (templates) except to add new templates.
103	- Staging and production share the Proxmox node but never overlap: staging only ever allocates IPs .50–.99 and ports 30000–30999. Never point staging pools at production ranges.
104	- Test risky/provisioning changes on staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh`) before promoting to production.
105	- Never `qm destroy` a VM that has a `Server` row — always go through a DELETE job.
106	- Never `pkill -f` by pattern on this box — kill by port PID or systemd unit instead (a pattern match has restarted live production before).
107	- Do not commit `.env`. Do not print the Proxmox token into logs or docs.
108	- Always `git commit` working states; never leave the tree broken — services restart from this directory.

1	// Pure pricing + guardrail math for CUSTOM VPS / game-server specs — servers
2	// bigger than the biggest premade plan ("Max"). No DB, no server-only imports:
3	// this is the ONE formula shared by the client-side deploy wizards (instant price
4	// as a slider moves, no round trip) and the server-side quote/order path
5	// (lib/custom-plan.ts, which re-validates everything here before a Plan row is
6	// ever created — a client-computed price is never trusted for money).
7	//
8	// ─── WHY "CUSTOM" EXISTS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9	// The premade ladder tops out at Max (4 vCPU / 16 GB / 120 GB). A customer who
10	// needs more than that on ANY dimension gets a one-off Plan row sized exactly to
11	// what they asked for (see lib/custom-plan.ts createCustomPlan) instead of being
12	// turned away or overpaying for a fixed "XL" tier that's still too small. So a
13	// valid custom spec is, by definition, Max-or-bigger on every dimension and
14	// STRICTLY bigger on at least one — never a way to buy something Max-sized (or
15	// smaller) at a different price, which would undercut the catalog and break the
16	// price-monotonic / disk-monotonic invariants lib/resize.ts depends on to keep
17	// upgrades honest.
18	//
19	// ─── PRICING FORMULA DERIVATION ──────────────────────────────────────────────
20	// The live ladder (prisma — Plan table) and its price DELTAS between adjacent
21	// tiers:
22	//
23	//   Tier      vCPU  RAM(GB)  Disk(GB)  Price      Δ vCPU  Δ RAM  Δ Disk  Δ Price
24	//   Starter     1      2        25     $8.88
25	//   Standard    2      4        50    $12.99        1       2      25    411¢
26	//   Pro         3      8        80    $20.99        1       4      30    800¢
27	//   Max         4     16       120    $32.99        1       8      40   1200¢
28	//
29	// A pure 3-variable linear fit (price = a·Δvcpu + b·Δram_GB + c·Δdisk_GB) across
30	// those three deltas turns out to be OVER-determined in a way the real ladder
31	// can't satisfy exactly: solving any two of the three delta-equations for
32	// (a, b, c) and checking against the third leaves a residual (405¢ vs 800¢ i.e
33	// disk-GB deltas here are exactly `20*Δvcpu + 2.5*Δram_GB`, so the three price
34	// points don't sit on a single consistent (a,b,c) — there's no clean 3-variable
35	// exact solution, only a best fit). So rather than force an unstable joint
36	// regression across three highly-correlated columns (cpu/ram/disk all grow
37	// together tier-to-tier), we ANCHOR the disk rate to a number the platform
38	// already charges for exactly this resource — `extra_disk_gb_price_cents`
39	// (lib/disk-expand.ts / lib/settings.ts), the live $0.10/GB/month a customer on
40	// ANY premade plan already pays to add root disk beyond their plan's included
41	// amount. Reusing it here means a GB of disk costs the same $ whether it comes
42	// from the extra-disk upsell or from building a custom plan — one number, one
43	// meaning, platform-wide.
44	//
45	// With disk fixed at that rate (10¢/GB), each tier-to-tier price delta minus its
46	// disk contribution attributes the REMAINDER to cpu + ram:
47	//
48	//   Standard-Starter: 411 - 10·25 = 161 = 1a + 2b
49	//   Pro-Standard:      800 - 10·30 = 500 = 1a + 4b
50	//   Max-Pro:          1200 - 10·40 = 800 = 1a + 8b
51	//
52	// Least-squares fit of those three (a, b) equations (normal equations
53	// 3a+14b=1461, 14a+84b=8722) solves EXACTLY to a = 11, b = 102 — i.e. $0.11 per
54	// extra vCPU/month and $1.02 per extra GB RAM/month. (RAM dominates the ladder's
55	// price growth far more than CPU does, which matches lib/capacity.ts's own
56	// framing of RAM as "the scarce resource" the platform oversells carefully
57	// while CPU is comparatively cheap to add.)

60	// `custom_plan_per_ram_gb_cents`; disk reuses the existing `extra_disk_gb_price_cents`)
61	// so the catalog can be retuned without a redeploy if the premade ladder ever moves.
62	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_DEFAULT_RATES: CustomPlanRates = {
63	  perVcpuCents: 11,
64	  perRamGbCents: 102,
65	  perDiskGbCents: 10, // mirrors extra_disk_gb_price_cents's shipped default
66	};

69	// `createCustomGamePlan` (lib/custom-plan.ts) used to reuse CUSTOM_PLAN_DEFAULT_RATES
70	// above UNMODIFIED for a GAME order — the pure VPS per-vCPU/per-RAM-GB rate, with no
71	// game-specific premium at all. Confirmed live against Rust: a real "Custom 10 vCPU /
72	// 23 GB" Rust order priced at $55.30/mo, barely above the standard 10 GB tier's
73	// $43.18/mo — a game server is materially more RAM-hungry per dollar than a plain VPS,
74	// and the flat VPS rate ($1.02/GB) didn't capture that at all. See the 2026-09-29
75	// DOCUMENTATION.md entry ("Custom game builds temporarily disabled") for the stop-gap
76	// this replaces.
77	//
78	// DERIVATION — same disk-anchoring + least-squares method as CUSTOM_PLAN_DEFAULT_RATES
79	// above, run per game family against its own live `GamePlan` ladder (prod `nxeon` DB,
80	// read 2026-09-29), with ONE necessary adaptation:
81	//
82	// The VPS ladder had 4 tiers (3 price deltas) to fit 2 unknowns (a=$/vCPU, b=$/RAM-GB)
83	// after anchoring disk — comfortably over-determined. Every game family has only 2-3
84	// tiers (1-2 deltas): as the task anticipated, "most families' tiers move RAM/CPU/disk
85	// together," so fitting BOTH a and b independently per family is either impossible (a
86	// single delta is 1 equation, 2 unknowns) or wildly unstable (solving the rare
87	// 2-delta/2-unknown families independently swings from a=-488¢ to a=+1590¢/vCPU
88	// depending on the family — see the derivation script's diagnostic output, kept at
89	// /root/nxeon-phase-custom-game-pricing/derive-rates.mjs for anyone re-deriving this
90	// later). So CPU is anchored too, the SAME way disk already is: pool the disk-anchored
91	// remainder across EVERY family's deltas, residualize out each family's own (unknown)
92	// RAM slope first (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell — regress both the CPU delta and the remainder
93	// on the RAM delta within each multi-delta family, keep only the leftover that RAM
94	// can't already explain), then fit ONE shared per-vCPU rate to what's left. That fit
95	// converges cleanly to $1.11/vCPU (82 pooled residual points from the 41 families with
96	// 3 real tiers) — close to, but a bit above, the VPS ladder's $0.11/vCPU, which is
97	// sensible: a ticking game-server process leans on its cores harder than idle VPS
98	// headroom does. With CPU (and disk) anchored, each family's own $/RAM-GB rate is then
99	// a clean, well-determined single-variable least-squares fit against its own real
100	// tiers — this is what actually varies 4x across the catalog (roughly $1.00/GB for a
101	// light title like ATS/ETS2 up to $4.63/GB for Conan) and is where each game's real
102	// pricing character lives.

104	// Every family currently in GAME_FAMILIES (lib/games.ts) with at least 2 live active
105	// GamePlan tiers as of 2026-09-29 got a real rate this way — all of them; the live
106	// catalog happens to have zero families with exactly 1 tier today. Two families

108	// rows at all (unseeded scaffolds — schedule1 has no official dedicated server to seed,

115	// second one ships, `estimatedGameFamilyRamRateCents` (lib/custom-plan.ts) covers that
116	// gap with a clearly-flagged genre-average estimate rather than inventing a number —
117	// see that function's own comment for why an estimate beats staying gated there
118	// specifically (unlike the zero-tier families above, a single real tier at least
119	// anchors the BASE price correctly; only the slope beyond it is a genre guess).

122	// (`custom_plan_game_per_vcpu_cents`); the per-family RAM-GB table lives in
123	// `custom_plan_game_ram_rates_json`, a JSON `{ family: cents }` override merged over

186	/**
187	 * Merge an admin JSON override (the `custom_plan_game_ram_rates_json` Setting) over
188	 * the derived default table. Pure and defensive — mirrors `parseRatesOverride`
189	 * (lib/currency.ts) exactly: unparseable JSON, a non-object payload, and any
190	 * non-positive/non-finite rate are all ignored so a fat-fingered override can only
191	 * fail SAFE (fall back to the derived default for that family), never zero out or
192	 * invert a game's price.
193	 */
194	export function parseGameFamilyRatesOverride(json: string | null | undefined): Record<string, number> {
195	  const rates: Record<string, number> = { ...CUSTOM_GAME_PLAN_DEFAULT_RAM_GB_CENTS };
196	  if (json && json.trim()) {
197	    try {
198	      const parsed = JSON.parse(json) as unknown;
199	      if (parsed && typeof parsed === "object" && !Array.isArray(parsed)) {
200	        for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(parsed as Record<string, unknown>)) {
201	          const family = k.trim();
202	          const rate = typeof v === "number" ? v : Number(v);
203	          if (family && Number.isFinite(rate) && rate > 0) rates[family] = Math.round(rate);
204	        }
205	      }
206	    } catch {
207	      // Malformed override -> defaults only. Never throws.
208	    }
209	  }
210	  return rates;

213	/** Sane platform-wide ceiling — deliberately generous (nothing in the premade
214	 *  catalog approaches this), but not infinite: a real physical node has to be
215	 *  able to hold it. Admin-tunable via lib/settings.ts (custom_plan_max_*). */
216	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_DEFAULT_CEILING: CustomPlanCeiling = {
217	  maxCpuCores: 32,
218	  maxRamMB: 128 * 1024,
219	  maxDiskGB: 2000,
220	};

222	/**
223	 * The `sortOrder` every one-off custom `Plan`/`GamePlan` row is created with (see
224	 * lib/custom-plan.ts). Shared here — a pure, dependency-free constant — so
225	 * lib/order.ts and lib/game-order.ts can recognize "this specific row is an
226	 * intentionally-inactive custom one-off, not a retired/disabled plan" without
227	 * either of them importing the DB-touching lib/custom-plan.ts. See the doc
228	 * comment on their `active` gates for why this matters: a custom plan is created
229	 * `active: false` so it stays invisible to the 30+ existing `where: { active: true }`
230	 * catalog/marketing/resize-picker queries across this codebase (none of which are
231	 * scoped to a single order or customer) — but it must still be a valid PURCHASE
232	 * TARGET for the one order that just built it.
233	 */
234	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_SORT_ORDER = 999;
235	
236	export type CustomPlanSpec = { cpuCores: number; ramMB: number; diskGB: number };
237	
238	/** The floor a custom spec must clear on every dimension — today, the live "Max"
239	 *  plan's specs (see lib/custom-plan.ts customPlanFloor, which reads it from the
240	 *  DB rather than hardcoding it, so a future catalog change is picked up live). */
241	export type CustomPlanFloor = {
242	  cpuCores: number;
243	  ramMB: number;
244	  diskGB: number;
245	  priceCents: number;
246	  bandwidthTB: number;
247	};
248	
249	export type CustomPlanCeiling = { maxCpuCores: number; maxRamMB: number; maxDiskGB: number };
250	
251	export type CustomPlanRates = { perVcpuCents: number; perRamGbCents: number; perDiskGbCents: number };
252	
253	/**
254	 * The custom-plan price: Max's price plus the per-unit rate for whatever exceeds
255	 * Max on each dimension. Only the EXCESS over the floor is charged for — a spec
256	 * that matches Max on RAM/disk but asks for double the CPU pays only for the
257	 * extra CPU, not a second copy of Max's whole price.
258	 *
259	 * Defensively clamped to STRICTLY more than the floor's price: a valid spec
260	 * (per validateCustomPlanSpec) always exceeds the floor on at least one
261	 * dimension, so with positive rates this clamp is a no-op — but if an admin ever
262	 * zeroes a rate (e.g. sets `extra_disk_gb_price_cents` to "0"), a disk-only
263	 * custom spec must still never price at-or-below Max, which would silently
264	 * undercut the catalog (the exact class of bug lib/resize.ts's price-monotonic
265	 * guard exists to prevent one level up, at resize time).
266	 */
267	export function computeCustomPlanPriceCents(
268	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
269	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
270	  rates: CustomPlanRates,
271	): number {
272	  const extraCpu = Math.max(0, spec.cpuCores - floor.cpuCores);
273	  const extraRamGB = Math.max(0, (spec.ramMB - floor.ramMB) / 1024);
274	  const extraDiskGB = Math.max(0, spec.diskGB - floor.diskGB);
275	  const raw =
276	    floor.priceCents +
277	    extraCpu * rates.perVcpuCents +
278	    extraRamGB * rates.perRamGbCents +
279	    extraDiskGB * rates.perDiskGbCents;
280	  return Math.max(Math.round(raw), floor.priceCents + 1);
281	}
282	
283	/** The one real, live tier this family's custom price is extrapolated FROM — its own
284	 *  biggest active `GamePlan` row (lib/custom-plan.ts resolves this from the DB; kept
285	 *  as a small anchor type here so the pure pricing math stays DB-free). */
286	export type CustomGamePlanAnchor = { cpuCores: number; ramMB: number; diskGB: number; priceCents: number };
287	
288	/**
289	 * The floor a custom GAME spec must clear — the VPS floor (today, Max) widened on any
290	 * dimension where this family's OWN top real tier is already bigger. Without this
291	 * widening, a family whose premade ladder already runs hotter than Max on some
292	 * dimension (e.g. Squad's top tier is 10 vCPU / 32 GB — both above Max's 4/16) could
293	 * have a "custom" order that is SMALLER than its own biggest premade tier on that
294	 * dimension while still clearing the generic VPS floor, which would both undercut that
295	 * tier's own price and violate the monotonic-upgrade invariant every other resize path
296	 * in this codebase depends on (see lib/resize.ts). `priceCents`/`bandwidthTB` stay the
297	 * VPS floor's — the anti-undercut price anchor is deliberately still the platform-wide
298	 * number here; `computeCustomGamePlanPriceCents` below does its own, family-curve-aware
299	 * pricing and re-clamps against this same VPS floor price directly.
300	 */
301	export function gameCustomFloor(vpsFloor: CustomPlanFloor, topTier: CustomGamePlanAnchor): CustomPlanFloor {
302	  return {
303	    cpuCores: Math.max(vpsFloor.cpuCores, topTier.cpuCores),
304	    ramMB: Math.max(vpsFloor.ramMB, topTier.ramMB),
305	    diskGB: Math.max(vpsFloor.diskGB, topTier.diskGB),
306	    priceCents: vpsFloor.priceCents,
307	    bandwidthTB: vpsFloor.bandwidthTB,
308	  };
309	}
310	
311	/**
312	 * The custom GAME price: this family's own top real tier's price, plus its own
313	 * per-vCPU/per-RAM-GB/per-disk-GB rate for whatever the spec asks beyond that tier —
314	 * literally extending the family's own real price curve past its last real data point,
315	 * rather than starting over from the flat VPS Max price the way the old (buggy)
316	 * behavior did. `dCpu`/`dRamGB`/`dDiskGB` can be negative on an individual dimension
317	 * (e.g. a spec at exactly `gameCustomFloor` for a family whose top tier already beat
318	 * Max on RAM will have `dRamGB` <= 0 there) — that's fine, it's still one evaluation of
319	 * the same straight line; only the FINAL price is clamped.
320	 *
321	 * Double-clamped, deliberately redundant with `gameCustomFloor`'s widening above: never
322	 * at-or-below the platform VPS-Max price (the same anti-undercut guarantee
323	 * `computeCustomPlanPriceCents` enforces for VPS), AND never at-or-below this family's
324	 * OWN top real tier's price. A caller that validated the spec against
325	 * `gameCustomFloor` first can never actually hit either clamp — they exist so this
326	 * function is safe on its own, not just in combination with that validation.
327	 */
328	export function computeCustomGamePlanPriceCents(
329	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
330	  topTier: CustomGamePlanAnchor,
331	  rates: CustomPlanRates,
332	  vpsFloorPriceCents: number,
333	): number {
334	  const dCpu = spec.cpuCores - topTier.cpuCores;
335	  const dRamGB = (spec.ramMB - topTier.ramMB) / 1024;
336	  const dDiskGB = spec.diskGB - topTier.diskGB;
337	  const raw =
338	    topTier.priceCents + dCpu * rates.perVcpuCents + dRamGB * rates.perRamGbCents + dDiskGB * rates.perDiskGbCents;
339	  return Math.max(Math.round(raw), vpsFloorPriceCents + 1, topTier.priceCents + 1);
340	}
341	
342	/**
343	 * Guardrails: every dimension must be at or above the floor (never a way to buy
344	 * something Max-sized or smaller under a different name) and at or below the
345	 * admin-configured ceiling. A spec that matches the floor EXACTLY on all three
346	 * dimensions is rejected too — that's just Max, not a custom order.
347	 */
348	export function validateCustomPlanSpec(
349	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
350	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
351	  ceiling: CustomPlanCeiling,
352	): { ok: true } | { ok: false; reason: string } {
353	  if (!Number.isFinite(spec.cpuCores) || !Number.isFinite(spec.ramMB) || !Number.isFinite(spec.diskGB)) {
354	    return { ok: false, reason: "Invalid configuration." };
355	  }
356	  if (spec.cpuCores < floor.cpuCores || spec.ramMB < floor.ramMB || spec.diskGB < floor.diskGB) {
357	    return {
358	      ok: false,
359	      reason:
360	        `A custom server can't go below ${floor.cpuCores} vCPU / ${floor.ramMB / 1024} GB RAM / ${floor.diskGB} GB disk ` +
361	        `on any dimension — for anything smaller, pick a plan above instead.`,
362	    };
363	  }
364	  if (spec.cpuCores > ceiling.maxCpuCores || spec.ramMB > ceiling.maxRamMB || spec.diskGB > ceiling.maxDiskGB) {
365	    return {
366	      ok: false,
367	      reason:
368	        `Custom servers top out at ${ceiling.maxCpuCores} vCPU / ${ceiling.maxRamMB / 1024} GB RAM / ` +
369	        `${ceiling.maxDiskGB} GB disk — contact support for anything larger.`,
370	    };
371	  }
372	  if (spec.cpuCores === floor.cpuCores && spec.ramMB === floor.ramMB && spec.diskGB === floor.diskGB) {
373	    return { ok: false, reason: "That's exactly the Max plan — choose Max above instead of building custom." };
374	  }
375	  return { ok: true };
376	}
377	
378	/** Clamp an arbitrary (e.g. slider-dragged, or player-count-derived) spec into the
379	 *  floor..ceiling range, rounding to whole units. Used by the UI so a slider or a
380	 *  recommendation can never even VISUALLY suggest an invalid spec. */
381	export function clampCustomPlanSpec(
382	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
383	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
384	  ceiling: CustomPlanCeiling,
385	): CustomPlanSpec {
386	  return {
387	    cpuCores: Math.min(ceiling.maxCpuCores, Math.max(floor.cpuCores, Math.round(spec.cpuCores))),
388	    ramMB: Math.min(ceiling.maxRamMB, Math.max(floor.ramMB, Math.round(spec.ramMB))),
389	    diskGB: Math.min(ceiling.maxDiskGB, Math.max(floor.diskGB, Math.round(spec.diskGB))),
390	  };
391	}
392	
393	/** Human name for the one-off Plan/GamePlan row this spec becomes. */
394	export function customPlanName(spec: CustomPlanSpec): string {
395	  const ramGB = Math.round(spec.ramMB / 1024);
396	  return `Custom ${spec.cpuCores} vCPU / ${ramGB} GB / ${spec.diskGB} GB Disk`;
397	}
398	
399	/** Slug pattern mirrors the one pre-existing manual precedent ("custom-4c8g-hmcebh")
400	 *  — short enough to stay under adminSavePlan's 30-char slug cap even at the
401	 *  ceiling's largest specs. `suffix` is a short random string the caller supplies
402	 *  (lib/custom-plan.ts) so this module stays free of any randomness/DB concerns. */
403	export function customPlanSlug(spec: CustomPlanSpec, suffix: string): string {
404	  const ramGB = Math.round(spec.ramMB / 1024);
405	  return `custom-${spec.cpuCores}c${ramGB}g-${suffix}`.slice(0, 30);
406	}
